name: Eyebrow darkener of gum arabic, ink and rosewater

card.summary: A historical homemade brow tint of gum arabic, ink and rosewater, used to darken sparse or pale eyebrows and frame the face.
card.note: Writing inks are not made for skin and were never tested as cosmetics; modern brow products are the regulated alternative.

quick.overview:
This is a do-it-yourself brow darkener from older beauty recipe tradition: ink for the colour, gum arabic to make it cling, and rosewater as a thinned, scented carrier. Brushed on, it makes light or thin brows look darker and fuller.

It survives as a historical curiosity rather than a documented product, and no studies of it exist.
quick.how: Historic recipes describe mixing the ingredients into a thin liquid and brushing it onto the brows with a small brush, where it dries as a stain-like film that lasts until washed or worn off.
quick.risks: General-purpose inks are not formulated or tested for skin or eye-area use, and some contain dyes or metals that can irritate or sensitise. Regulators approve specific colour additives for the eye area, and dermatologists generally recommend products made for that purpose.

lead: The eyebrow darkener of gum arabic, ink and rosewater is a homemade brow tint associated with historical beauty recipes. Its aim is cosmetic: darker, more defined brows that frame the eyes.

Gum arabic is a natural gum harvested from Acacia trees that dissolves in water; cosmetics and pharmaceuticals use it as a binder, emulsifier and suspending agent, and inks use it for viscosity control.[1] In this recipe it holds the pigment in place on the hair, with rosewater as the liquid.

Darkening the eyes and brows has a long history. Kohl, traditionally made from crushed stibnite, has been worn in Egypt since about 3100 BCE, and lead-based versions have been linked to elevated blood lead.[2] No clinical studies of this specific mixture exist.

chain: Gum arabic binds the colour to the hairs and skin
angle.text: The mixture tints pale or sparse brows so they look darker and better defined, a result any modern brow pencil or tint also aims for.

paras: Gum arabic is a mixture of glycoproteins and polysaccharides from Acacia trees, with about 70% of the world supply from Sudan, and it is generally recognised as safe as a dietary fibre.[1] That safety status applies to eating it, not to any ink it is mixed with.
Eye and brow darkeners such as kohl are among the oldest cosmetics, used in Egypt from roughly 3100 BCE and elsewhere across Africa, the Middle East and South Asia.[2]

Traditional kohl products containing lead have been associated with higher blood lead levels, and the US FDA does not list kohl as an approved colour additive.[2] Writing inks are not cosmetic-grade, so their ingredients vary.
